methodology.title: Methodology
methodology.intro: How Forecast Arena collects forecasts, defines truth, and scores the models, and where the numbers stop being trustworthy.

sources.title: Sources
sources.body:
Nine numerical models come from the Open-Meteo forecast API and one from MET Norway’s Locationforecast. Every value is placed on a 6-hour UTC grid (00, 06, 12, 18). Temperature, wind and pressure are the values at the step; precipitation is the total of the six hours ending at the step.
Regional models return data only inside their domain, so a city outside Europe shows up to eight models.

truth.title: Truth
truth.body:
Truth is model analysis, not station observations. For each 6-hour step the analysis of a model is its own forecast from the most recent run (0 to 6 hours lead), taken from Open-Meteo’s archive of previous runs.
Consensus truth, the default, is the median of those analyses when at least {contributors} models contribute. Self-analysis scores each model against its own analysis, which rewards consistency rather than accuracy.

skill.title: Skill
skill.body:
For each model and lead bucket (24, 48, 72, 96 hours: runs issued one to four days earlier) the scoreboard reports mean absolute error, bias (forecast minus truth), root mean square error and the number of samples. Precipitation adds a hit rate: forecast and truth both above or both below {hit} mm in the 6-hour step.
Cells with fewer than {minN} samples are hatched and excluded from the ranking. Windows of 7, 30 and 90 days aggregate every 6-hour step in the window.

disagreement.title: Disagreement
disagreement.body: For temperature, wind and pressure the daily disagreement is the average, over the day’s future steps, of the spread between the highest and the lowest model. For precipitation it is the range of the models’ daily totals. Days are in the city’s local time. Thresholds:

limits.title: Limits
limits.body: Model values are grid-point values, not the weather at a street corner, and the models’ own analyses share their biases. MET Norway keeps no archive, so it is not scored until scheduled runs accumulate. This prototype stores data in local JSON files and caches in memory; the production design uses Postgres, Redis and S3.
